slides.title: Modern HTTPS uses two types of encryption

blocks.content: Modern HTTPS relies on **asymmetric cryptography** during the TLS handshake, but switches to **symmetric encryption** for performance. Protocols like TLS use algorithms such as RSA or ECDHE for key exchange, then fall back to fast ciphers like AES for bulk data encryption.

slides.title: DNS was never designed with security in mind

blocks.content: DNS was never designed with security in mind, which led to attacks like **cache poisoning**. Extensions like DNSSEC add authenticity via digital signatures, but adoption is still uneven across domains and resolvers.

slides.title: Many exploits target control data on the stack

blocks.content: Many memory corruption exploits rely on overwriting control data like **return addresses** on the stack. Defenses such as **Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR)** and **Data Execution Prevention (DEP)** make exploitation significantly harder — but not impossible.

slides.title: Never use fast hash functions for passwords

blocks.content: Password hashing should never use fast hash functions like MD5 or SHA-1. Modern systems rely on **adaptive hashing algorithms** like bcrypt or Argon2 that are intentionally slow and resistant to GPU-based brute force attacks.

The concept of **"zero trust"** security assumes no implicit trust within a network. Frameworks like Zero Trust Architecture enforce **continuous authentication**, authorization, and device posture checks — even for internal traffic.

slides.title: Secrets can leak without breaking encryption

blocks.content: Side-channel attacks can extract secrets **without breaking encryption mathematically**. Attacks targeting implementations of AES or RSA can use timing, power consumption, or cache behavior to leak keys.
